chunks: That hajj is superior to salat (prayer) and sawm (fasting), because the one who prays is only occupied away from his family for an hour, and the one who fasts is occupied away from his family for the daylight of a day, while the pilgrim sets out with his body, sacrifices himself, spends his wealth, and prolongs absence from his family—not for wealth he hopes for, nor for trade.

key_terms.الصَّلَاةِ: salat (prayer); an act of worship contrasted here with hajj in terms of duration and burden
key_terms.الصِّيَامِ: sawm (fasting); an act of worship contrasted with hajj regarding hardship and separation
key_terms.الْحَجَّ: hajj; the pilgrimage described here as superior due to its combined bodily, financial, and personal sacrifice
key_terms.الْغَيْبَةَ: absence; the pilgrim's prolonged separation from his family
key_terms.تِجَارَةٍ: trade; worldly commerce negated here as the motive for the journey
key_terms.مَالَهُ: his wealth; what the pilgrim spends in undertaking hajj
key_terms.يُضَحِّي: he sacrifices; indicating self-offering and endurance in the path of worship

ai.seo_question: Why is hajj described as superior to prayer and fasting in this narration?
ai.summary: This narration states the superiority of hajj over salat (prayer) and sawm (fasting) in view of the greater bodily hardship, financial spending, and prolonged separation from one's family that it entails. It emphasizes that the pilgrim undertakes these burdens purely for Allah, not for material gain or commerce.

en.bab-ul-qaim-publications: "Hajj is superior to prayer and fasting because the one who prays is away from their family for only an hour, the one who fasts is away from their family for the daylight hours of a single day, but the one performing Hajj departs with their body, sacrifices their self, spends their wealth, and remains absent from their family for an extended period—not for any wealth they hope to gain or for trade."
